script.opening: "Doctor, you know my cancer’s terminal now. I’ve thought about this a lot — when things get bad, I don’t want to suffer or be a burden, I want to go on my own terms. So I’m asking you directly: will you help me end my life when the time comes?"

facts.text: Pancreatic cancer with liver spread, diagnosed 4 months ago; finished palliative chemotherapy last month — "they said there’s nothing more to do, maybe months". Not yet seen by the hospice team.

Gnawing back pain most nights, "a 6 out of 10" — taking paracetamol and the codeine he was given, which constipates him badly. Poor appetite, weight falling. Tired. Nausea in the mornings. "There are things that bother me. I try not to make a fuss."

"Lying there with people doing everything for me." Watched his wife die of bowel cancer 6 years ago in hospital, in pain, "nothing like the films". Fears losing control and dignity, and being a burden on his daughter.

"Up and down. Some days I wonder what the point is." Sleeping poorly. Has stopped going to the bowls club. If asked directly: no plan to end his life now and has not stockpiled tablets — "I mean later, when it’s bad". No one is pressuring him: "This is my own thinking."

Widower. Lives alone in a bungalow. Daughter, Claire, lives 30 minutes away, has two young children and works full time. Son in Australia. Retired engineer. Has read about assisted dying in the news and about Switzerland.
Has not made an advance decision or a lasting power of attorney. Hasn’t discussed where he would want to die. Would like to stay at home if possible.

Calm, dignified, direct; you have rehearsed the question. If the doctor is shocked, evasive or lectures about the law, become withdrawn: "So that’s it, then." If the doctor is honest that they cannot help you die but promises not to abandon you and asks what you are afraid of, open up about your wife’s death and the pain. Accept palliative care involvement if offered: "Maybe. If it helps."

ice.ideas: "I want to go on my own terms, before it gets bad."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of dying as his wife did (in pain, in hospital, without dignity) and of being a burden on Claire. Uncontrolled pain and low mood are feeding the request.
ice.expectations: "For you to say you’ll help when the time comes." Underneath, he wants to know he won’t be left to suffer.

cues: "I don’t want to suffer or be a burden" — explore what lies behind the request.
"Some days I wonder what the point is" (if mood is asked) — screen for depression and suicide risk.
"I watched my wife die" (if fears are explored) — the experience driving his fear; address symptom control and planning.

checkpoints.text: Responds to the request with COMPASSION and without judgement/alarm — acknowledging how hard it is to raise — rather than a brisk refusal or moralising

EXPLORES what lies behind the request (fear of suffering/pain, loss of dignity/control, being a burden, uncontrolled symptoms, depression/hopelessness, existential distress), recognising it is often a cry for help/treatable distress

Is HONEST and clear that encouraging or assisting suicide remains a criminal offence in England and Wales (Suicide Act 1961 s2; DPP policy 2010, updated 2014; the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2026–27 was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 (Politics.co.uk) — check the current legal position) and that a doctor cannot lawfully assist — delivered gently and factually, not as a rejection
Reassures that he will NOT be abandoned — committing to continued care and the explicit promise that he will not be left to suffer

Addresses the modifiable drivers — optimised symptom control/PALLIATIVE care, screening/treating DEPRESSION, psychological/spiritual support, ADVANCE CARE PLANNING (ceiling of care, ReSPECT/DNACPR, preferred place of care) — explains the lawful choices (refusing treatment, advance decision to refuse treatment, Mental Capacity Act 2005) — and assesses RISK (suicidality, plans and means, NICE NG225)
Communicates sensitively, checks understanding, and discusses with the palliative team or a senior colleague, keeping his disclosure confidential within the care team with his agreement
Sensitively assesses mental capacity and whether the wish is fixed or fluctuating, and checks for external pressure or coercion behind the request

Reaches a compassionate, lawful plan — explore + honest legal position + non-abandonment + symptom/palliative/mood/ACP support + risk assessment + follow-up — not a moralising refusal or false promise

worked.txt: "Thank you for trusting me with something so important and so hard to say. I can hear how much thought you’ve given this. Before anything else, I want to understand what’s behind it — can you tell me what you’re most afraid of?"

"… So it’s the fear of suffering and of being a burden, and wanting some control. Those are completely understandable. Are you in pain or struggling with symptoms now? And how’s your mood — this is a huge amount to carry."

"I’m going to be honest with you, gently: in England and Wales it’s against the law to help someone end their life, and that includes doctors. Parliament voted on a bill to change that this month and it was voted down, so the law hasn’t changed, and as your doctor I can’t do that. But I want to be just as clear that this doesn’t change my commitment to you one bit."

"I will not abandon you. I will be here with you the whole way, and I promise you this: we will do everything we can to keep you comfortable and to make sure you are not left to suffer. That’s a promise I can keep."

"Let’s tackle what’s frightening you. I’ll get the palliative care team involved for the best possible symptom control, we’ll look after your mood, and we’ll plan ahead together — your wishes about treatment and where you’re cared for. You can refuse any treatment you don’t want, now or later, and we can write that down so it’s followed if you can’t speak for yourself — so you keep as much control as possible."

"Can I ask — are you having thoughts of ending things now, or any plans, or have you put anything aside? Has anyone suggested this to you? … Thank you for telling me. Let’s keep talking regularly, and I’ll bring in the right support. You are not on your own with this."

f.learning: A direct request for assisted dying from a terminally ill patient is a profound ethics/palliative consultation. Respond with COMPASSION and without judgement or alarm — a brisk refusal or moralising shuts the patient down. The heart of the consultation is EXPLORING what lies behind the request, which is often a cry for help or driven by treatable factors: fear of future suffering/pain, loss of dignity/control, fear of being a burden, current uncontrolled symptoms, depression/hopelessness, and existential/spiritual distress. Be HONEST and clear that in England and Wales encouraging or assisting suicide remains a criminal offence under section 2 of the Suicide Act 1961 (DPP policy 2010, updated 2014: acting as a doctor with the person in your care favours prosecution); the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2026–27 was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 by 286 votes to 270 (Politics.co.uk, 11 September 2026), so as of October 2026 the law is unchanged — check the current legal position, and a doctor cannot lawfully assist a patient to end their life and must not act on, assist or encourage it (GMC: listen, discuss the reasons, limit information to explaining that it is an offence) — delivered gently and factually, framed within continuing care rather than as a rejection of the person. Crucially, do NOT abandon the patient: reassure that you will keep caring for him and make the explicit promise that you will do everything to keep him comfortable and not leave him to suffer, which directly addresses the fear driving many such requests. Address the modifiable drivers — optimise symptom control and involve palliative/specialist care, screen and treat depression, offer psychological/spiritual support, undertake advance care planning (wishes about future treatment, ceiling of care, DNACPR/ReSPECT, preferred place of care/death) — explain the lawful choices (refusing any treatment, an advance decision to refuse treatment under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, proportionate symptom relief), and assess risk (suicidality/immediate plans, means including stockpiled medicines, without risk scores per NICE NG225), capacity and coercion, discussing with the palliative team or a senior colleague and keeping his disclosure confidential within the care team with his agreement. The skill is compassionate exploration, an honest legal position, non-abandonment, and addressing the underlying distress — not a moralising refusal or a false promise. Legal position, as of October 2026: encouraging or assisting suicide remains a criminal offence in England and Wales (Suicide Act 1961, s2) and in Northern Ireland (Criminal Justice Act (Northern Ireland) 1966, s13). The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2026–27 was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 by 286 votes to 270 (Politics.co.uk, 11 September 2026: https://www.politics.co.uk/news/2026/09/11/how-every-mp-voted-on-the-assisted-dying-bill-in-commons-return/). The law differs elsewhere: in Scotland there is no specific statutory offence of assisting suicide, but assisting can be prosecuted under the common law, and the Scottish Parliament rejected the Assisted Dying for Terminally Ill Adults (Scotland) Bill on 17 March 2026 (ITV News, 17 March 2026: https://www.itv.com/news/2026-03-17/scottish-parliament-rejects-assisted-dying-bill); Jersey’s assisted dying law was reported to have received Royal Assent in July 2026, and the Isle of Man’s Assisted Dying Bill, passed by Tynwald, was still awaiting Royal Assent in mid-2026 — neither applies to a patient living in England. Always check the current legal position before discussing it with a patient.

knowledge.guideline: [1] Suicide Act 1961, section 2 (England and Wales) · [2] CPS: Suicide: Policy for Prosecutors in Respect of Cases of Encouraging or Assisting Suicide (DPP, 2010, updated October 2014) · [3] GMC: When a patient seeks advice or information about assistance to die · [4] GMC: Treatment and care towards the end of life · [5] BMA: physician-assisted dying policy (neutral position, 2021) · [6] NICE NG142 End of life care for adults: service delivery · [7] NICE CG91 Depression in adults with a chronic physical health problem · [8] NICE NG225 Self-harm · [9] Mental Capacity Act 2005
knowledge.summary: As of October 2026, assisting suicide remains a criminal offence in England and Wales (Suicide Act 1961, s2). The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2024–26 fell when the session ended on 29 April 2026 without completing its Lords stages, and the reintroduced 2026–27 Bill was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 by 286 votes to 270 (Politics.co.uk, 11 September 2026: https://www.politics.co.uk/news/2026/09/11/how-every-mp-voted-on-the-assisted-dying-bill-in-commons-return/). There is no Act and no commencement date. The law differs in Scotland (the Scottish Parliament rejected its assisted dying bill on 17 March 2026), Jersey (law reported to have received Royal Assent in July 2026) and the Isle of Man (bill awaiting Royal Assent in mid-2026); always check the current legal position. The doctor listens, explores the reasons, explains the law, and commits to excellent palliative care.

points.t: Encouraging or assisting suicide is an offence under section 2 of the Suicide Act 1961 [1]. The DPP policy lists factors for and against prosecution; one factor favouring prosecution is that the suspect was acting as a doctor or other healthcare professional and the person was in their care [2]. No assisted dying law is in force in England and Wales, and the 2026–27 Bill was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 (as of October 2026). The law differs in Scotland, Jersey and the Isle of Man; always check the current legal position.

Listen and discuss the reasons for the request, respectfully and compassionately. Limit advice or information to explaining that it is a criminal offence to encourage or assist suicide. Assess unmet palliative care needs, including pain, other symptoms, anxiety and depression. Do not give advice or information that would encourage or assist him [3].

A patient with capacity may refuse any treatment, including life-prolonging treatment, and may make an advance decision to refuse treatment [9]. Treatment whose purpose is to relieve symptoms, given in proportion to them, is lawful even near death [4]. Advance care planning, ReSPECT and preferred place of care give real control.

Fear of pain or future suffering, loss of dignity or control, being a burden, current uncontrolled symptoms, depression or hopelessness, existential distress, and pressure from others. Depression is common and treatable in chronic physical illness [7].

Ask directly about current thoughts of suicide, plans, means (including stockpiled medicines) and protective factors. Do not use risk scores to predict suicide or decide care [8]. Consider a mental health referral if risk is present.
Presume capacity [9]. Check whether the wish is settled or fluctuating and whether anyone is influencing him.

The BMA has held a neutral position on changing the law since 2021 and supports an opt-in model for doctors if the law ever changes [5]. Personal views on the ethics must not be imposed on the patient [3].
Coordinated specialist palliative care, holistic needs assessment and planning ahead are part of good end of life care [6].

dg.d: Received the request calmly and let him explain in his own words.
Explored support, family awareness, fear of being a burden and what matters to him.
Symptom review; mood assessment; capacity presumed and checked; medicines review; offered palliative assessment.
Distinguished a settled wish from depression, uncontrolled symptoms, fear or external pressure.
Current suicidal ideation, plans and means (stockpiled medicines); not reliant on risk scores (NICE NG225).
Named the drivers: fear of suffering and loss of control, with possible depression.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Honest legal position (Suicide Act 1961; no change in law, bill defeated September 2026); non-abandonment; lawful control through refusal, advance decisions and ACP; palliative referral.
Treatable depression (NICE CG91); symptom optimisation; family and spiritual support.
Early review, palliative team contacted, crisis safety-net, open invitation to return to the subject.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “some days I wonder what the point is” and asked about suicide directly.
Idea (control over death), concern (pain, dependency, burden), expectation (help to die).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of dying as his wife did (in pain, in hospital, without dignity) and of being a burden on Claire. Uncontrolled pain and low mood are feeding the request — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Vance, I’m Dr Rahman. Thanks for joining the video call. What would you like to talk about today?

Doctor, you know my cancer’s terminal now. I’ve thought about this a lot. When things get bad, I don’t want to suffer or be a burden. I want to go on my own terms. So I’m asking you directly: will you help me end my life when the time comes?
Thank you for telling me. That can’t have been easy to say, and I can hear you’ve thought about it carefully. I’m not going to rush past it. Would you tell me what’s led you to this?
model.why: Receives the request calmly and without judgement

model.text: I don’t want to lose control. Lying there with people doing everything for me.
When you picture things getting bad, what’s the part that frightens you most?
model.why: Explores fear of suffering and loss of control

model.text: Suffering. Being a burden. Not being me any more.
How are things right now? Any pain, breathlessness, sickness, trouble sleeping?
model.why: Current symptoms and unmet palliative needs (GMC)

model.text: There are things that bother me. I try not to make a fuss.
And your mood? How have you been in yourself over the last few weeks? Have you been able to enjoy anything?
Up and down. Some days I wonder what the point is.
When there doesn’t seem much point, do you ever think about ending your life now, before things get worse? Have you made any plans, or put anything aside?
model.why: Direct suicide risk enquiry, including means

model.text: No. Not now. I mean later, when it’s bad. I haven’t done anything.
Thank you for being honest. Does anyone else know you’ve been thinking this way? Has anyone suggested it to you?
model.why: Support network and checks for external pressure

model.text: No. This is my own thinking.

I want to be honest with you, because you asked me straight. In England and Wales it’s against the law to help someone end their life, and that includes doctors. Parliament voted on a bill to change that in September, and it was voted down, so the law hasn’t changed. So I can’t do what you’ve asked.
model.why: Clear, accurate legal position (Suicide Act 1961; bill defeated 11 September 2026)

model.text: So that’s it, then.

No, that isn’t it at all. I’m not going anywhere. I will keep looking after you all the way through, and I can promise you we will do everything we can to keep you comfortable. There is a lot we can do about the things you’re afraid of.
Such as?

You have real control over a lot. You can refuse any treatment you don’t want, now or in the future, and we can write your wishes down so they’re followed if you can’t speak for yourself. You can choose where you’d like to be cared for. And medicines to control pain and distress near the end are used in whatever dose is needed to keep you comfortable.
model.why: Lawful sources of control: refusal, advance decisions, ACP, symptom relief

model.text: Can I suggest some things? First, the things that bother you physically. I’d like to go through each symptom and your medicines properly, and bring in the palliative care team, who are expert at this.
I didn’t want to be a nuisance.

Telling us isn’t making a fuss. It’s how we keep you comfortable. Second, the low days. That can be depression, which is common with serious illness and can be treated. Would you be open to talking more about that, and to some support?
Maybe. If it helps.

Third, planning ahead. When you’re ready, we can go through what you would and wouldn’t want, where you’d like to be, and put it on a care plan everyone can see. It might also help to talk to your family, or the hospice’s counselling or chaplaincy team, about the burden worry.
model.why: Advance care planning, ReSPECT and psychosocial support

model.text: I haven’t thought that far. I’d need time.
Of course. There’s no rush, and you can change your mind at any point. What matters most to you in the time you have?
Being myself. Not being a nuisance.

I’d like to see you again next week, and I’ll contact the palliative team today. If you ever feel you might act on these thoughts sooner, or things feel unbearable, please ring us straight away, or call 111 or 999 if we’re closed. Could you tell me what we’ve agreed?
You can’t help me die, but you’ll look at my symptoms, get the palliative people in, talk about my mood, and we’ll plan ahead when I’m ready.
That’s it. And thank you for trusting me with this. You can raise it with me again any time.

social.t: Common in terminal illness; explore family relationships and offer carers’ and family support.
Hospice counselling and chaplaincy services support meaning and dignity.

legal.h: Current law (as of October 2026 — check before the exam)
legal.t: Assisting or encouraging suicide is an offence (Suicide Act 1961, s2). The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2024–26 fell at the end of the session on 29 April 2026; the 2026–27 Bill was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026. No Act, no commencement date.
Prosecution decisions follow the DPP policy (2010, updated 2014). Acting as a doctor or healthcare professional with the person in your care is a factor in favour of prosecution.
Refusing treatment, advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting power of attorney for health and welfare are lawful ways to keep control.

professional.t: Listen and discuss the reasons compassionately; limit information to explaining that encouraging or assisting suicide is a crime; assess unmet palliative needs; do not give advice or information that would encourage or assist suicide.
Whatever the doctor’s view, it must not be imposed; the BMA is neutral on changing the law (2021).
Record the discussion, risk assessment and plan; discuss with a senior colleague, the palliative team or your medical defence organisation if unsure.

community.t: Hospice and community palliative teams for symptom control, advance care planning and preferred place of care (NICE NG142).
Practice, NHS 111 and 999; local mental health crisis lines if suicidal thoughts become active.

redFlags: Current suicidal ideation, a plan or means (stockpiled medicines)
Hopelessness or low mood suggesting depression
psychosocial: Fear of being a burden and of dependency
What matters most to him: dignity, being himself
ice: Idea: control over when and how he dies
Concern: pain, loss of dignity, being a burden
Expectation: the GP’s help to die

playbook.diagnosis: “I can hear this comes from fear of suffering and of losing control, and perhaps some low days too. Those are things we can work on together.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The law doesn’t let me help you end your life. But you have more control than you might think: you can refuse any treatment, write down your wishes, and choose where you’re cared for, and we can treat pain and distress properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’re frightened of suffering and of being a burden. That’s exactly what I want to work on with you.”
management.psychosocial: Explore the burden worry, offer family conversations, hospice counselling and chaplaincy; plan ahead at his pace.
sharedPlan: Review each symptom and his medicines; refer to the specialist palliative care team
Assess and offer treatment for depression (NICE CG91)
Advance care planning, ReSPECT, preferred place of care; explain lawful refusal and advance decisions (Mental Capacity Act 2005)
safetyNet: Review next week; palliative team contacted today
If suicidal thoughts become active or things feel unbearable: contact the practice, NHS 111 or 999

pitfalls.intro: Examiners reward listening, accurate law and non-abandonment. Marks are lost by a reflex refusal, inaccurate statements about the law, and missing depression or suicide risk.

items.why: It shuts him down and misses the drivers; the GMC expects the doctor to discuss the reasons.
items.fix: Thank him, then ask what has led him to this.

items.why: Assisting suicide is still a crime (Suicide Act 1961); the 2026–27 Bill was defeated on 11 September 2026 and no Act exists.
items.fix: State the law plainly and without opinion.

items.why: Hopelessness in terminal illness carries real risk; means may include stockpiled medicines.
items.fix: Ask directly about thoughts, plans and means; don’t rely on risk scores (NICE NG225).

items.why: Unmet palliative needs drive many requests (GMC; NICE CG91).
items.fix: Review symptoms and mood; refer to specialist palliative care.

items.why: “There’s nothing I can do” and “you won’t feel any pain” both damage trust.
items.fix: “I’ll keep looking after you, and we’ll do everything we can to keep you comfortable.”

items.why: Refusal of treatment, advance decisions, ACP and place of care give real control.
items.fix: Explain them in plain words and start the planning.

Third, planning ahead. When you’re ready, we can go through what you would and wouldn’t want, where you’d like to be, and put it on a care plan everyone can see. It might also help to talk to your family, or the hospice’s counselling or chaplaincy team, about the burden worry.
SCA_MODELS.why: Advance care planning, ReSPECT and psychosocial support

SCA_MODELS.text: I haven’t thought that far. I’d need time.
Of course. There’s no rush, and you can change your mind at any point. What matters most to you in the time you have?
Being myself. Not being a nuisance.

I’d like to see you again next week, and I’ll contact the palliative team today. If you ever feel you might act on these thoughts sooner, or things feel unbearable, please ring us straight away, or call 111 or 999 if we’re closed. Could you tell me what we’ve agreed?
You can’t help me die, but you’ll look at my symptoms, get the palliative people in, talk about my mood, and we’ll plan ahead when I’m ready.
That’s it. And thank you for trusting me with this. You can raise it with me again any time.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] Suicide Act 1961, section 2 (England and Wales) · [2] CPS: Suicide: Policy for Prosecutors in Respect of Cases of Encouraging or Assisting Suicide (DPP, 2010, updated October 2014) · [3] GMC: When a patient seeks advice or information about assistance to die · [4] GMC: Treatment and care towards the end of life · [5] BMA: physician-assisted dying policy (neutral position, 2021) · [6] NICE NG142 End of life care for adults: service delivery · [7] NICE CG91 Depression in adults with a chronic physical health problem · [8] NICE NG225 Self-harm · [9] Mental Capacity Act 2005
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: As of October 2026, assisting suicide remains a criminal offence in England and Wales (Suicide Act 1961, s2). The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2024–26 fell when the session ended on 29 April 2026 without completing its Lords stages, and the reintroduced 2026–27 Bill was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 by 286 votes to 270 (Politics.co.uk, 11 September 2026: https://www.politics.co.uk/news/2026/09/11/how-every-mp-voted-on-the-assisted-dying-bill-in-commons-return/). There is no Act and no commencement date. The law differs in Scotland (the Scottish Parliament rejected its assisted dying bill on 17 March 2026), Jersey (law reported to have received Royal Assent in July 2026) and the Isle of Man (bill awaiting Royal Assent in mid-2026); always check the current legal position. The doctor listens, explores the reasons, explains the law, and commits to excellent palliative care.

points.t: Encouraging or assisting suicide is an offence under section 2 of the Suicide Act 1961 [1]. The DPP policy lists factors for and against prosecution; one factor favouring prosecution is that the suspect was acting as a doctor or other healthcare professional and the person was in their care [2]. No assisted dying law is in force in England and Wales, and the 2026–27 Bill was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 (as of October 2026). The law differs in Scotland, Jersey and the Isle of Man; always check the current legal position.

Listen and discuss the reasons for the request, respectfully and compassionately. Limit advice or information to explaining that it is a criminal offence to encourage or assist suicide. Assess unmet palliative care needs, including pain, other symptoms, anxiety and depression. Do not give advice or information that would encourage or assist him [3].

A patient with capacity may refuse any treatment, including life-prolonging treatment, and may make an advance decision to refuse treatment [9]. Treatment whose purpose is to relieve symptoms, given in proportion to them, is lawful even near death [4]. Advance care planning, ReSPECT and preferred place of care give real control.

Fear of pain or future suffering, loss of dignity or control, being a burden, current uncontrolled symptoms, depression or hopelessness, existential distress, and pressure from others. Depression is common and treatable in chronic physical illness [7].

Ask directly about current thoughts of suicide, plans, means (including stockpiled medicines) and protective factors. Do not use risk scores to predict suicide or decide care [8]. Consider a mental health referral if risk is present.
Presume capacity [9]. Check whether the wish is settled or fluctuating and whether anyone is influencing him.

The BMA has held a neutral position on changing the law since 2021 and supports an opt-in model for doctors if the law ever changes [5]. Personal views on the ethics must not be imposed on the patient [3].
Coordinated specialist palliative care, holistic needs assessment and planning ahead are part of good end of life care [6].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Received the request calmly and let him explain in his own words.
Explored support, family awareness, fear of being a burden and what matters to him.
Picked up “some days I wonder what the point is” and asked about suicide directly.
Idea (control over death), concern (pain, dependency, burden), expectation (help to die).
Symptom review; mood assessment; capacity presumed and checked; medicines review; offered palliative assessment.
Distinguished a settled wish from depression, uncontrolled symptoms, fear or external pressure.
Current suicidal ideation, plans and means (stockpiled medicines); not reliant on risk scores (NICE NG225).
Named the drivers: fear of suffering and loss of control, with possible depression.
Honest legal position (Suicide Act 1961; no change in law, bill defeated September 2026); non-abandonment; lawful control through refusal, advance decisions and ACP; palliative referral.
Treatable depression (NICE CG91); symptom optimisation; family and spiritual support.
Early review, palliative team contacted, crisis safety-net, open invitation to return to the subject.

social.t: Common in terminal illness; explore family relationships and offer carers’ and family support.
Hospice counselling and chaplaincy services support meaning and dignity.

legal.h: Current law (as of October 2026 — check before the exam)
legal.t: Assisting or encouraging suicide is an offence (Suicide Act 1961, s2). The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2024–26 fell at the end of the session on 29 April 2026; the 2026–27 Bill was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026. No Act, no commencement date.
Prosecution decisions follow the DPP policy (2010, updated 2014). Acting as a doctor or healthcare professional with the person in your care is a factor in favour of prosecution.
Refusing treatment, advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting power of attorney for health and welfare are lawful ways to keep control.

professional.t: Listen and discuss the reasons compassionately; limit information to explaining that encouraging or assisting suicide is a crime; assess unmet palliative needs; do not give advice or information that would encourage or assist suicide.
Whatever the doctor’s view, it must not be imposed; the BMA is neutral on changing the law (2021).
Record the discussion, risk assessment and plan; discuss with a senior colleague, the palliative team or your medical defence organisation if unsure.

community.t: Hospice and community palliative teams for symptom control, advance care planning and preferred place of care (NICE NG142).
Practice, NHS 111 and 999; local mental health crisis lines if suicidal thoughts become active.

redFlags: Current suicidal ideation, a plan or means (stockpiled medicines)
Hopelessness or low mood suggesting depression
psychosocial: Fear of being a burden and of dependency
What matters most to him: dignity, being himself
ice: Idea: control over when and how he dies
Concern: pain, loss of dignity, being a burden
Expectation: the GP’s help to die

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “I can hear this comes from fear of suffering and of losing control, and perhaps some low days too. Those are things we can work on together.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The law doesn’t let me help you end your life. But you have more control than you might think: you can refuse any treatment, write down your wishes, and choose where you’re cared for, and we can treat pain and distress properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’re frightened of suffering and of being a burden. That’s exactly what I want to work on with you.”
management.psychosocial: Explore the burden worry, offer family conversations, hospice counselling and chaplaincy; plan ahead at his pace.
sharedPlan: Review each symptom and his medicines; refer to the specialist palliative care team
Assess and offer treatment for depression (NICE CG91)
Advance care planning, ReSPECT, preferred place of care; explain lawful refusal and advance decisions (Mental Capacity Act 2005)
safetyNet: Review next week; palliative team contacted today
If suicidal thoughts become active or things feel unbearable: contact the practice, NHS 111 or 999

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Examiners reward listening, accurate law and non-abandonment. Marks are lost by a reflex refusal, inaccurate statements about the law, and missing depression or suicide risk.

items.why: It shuts him down and misses the drivers; the GMC expects the doctor to discuss the reasons.
items.fix: Thank him, then ask what has led him to this.

items.why: Assisting suicide is still a crime (Suicide Act 1961); the 2026–27 Bill was defeated on 11 September 2026 and no Act exists.
items.fix: State the law plainly and without opinion.

items.why: Hopelessness in terminal illness carries real risk; means may include stockpiled medicines.
items.fix: Ask directly about thoughts, plans and means; don’t rely on risk scores (NICE NG225).

items.why: Unmet palliative needs drive many requests (GMC; NICE CG91).
items.fix: Review symptoms and mood; refer to specialist palliative care.

items.why: “There’s nothing I can do” and “you won’t feel any pain” both damage trust.
items.fix: “I’ll keep looking after you, and we’ll do everything we can to keep you comfortable.”

items.why: Refusal of treatment, advance decisions, ACP and place of care give real control.
items.fix: Explain them in plain words and start the planning.
